episodes.title: The Coming El Niño with Michael Ferrari
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Michael Ferrari (Mobey research) argues the current El Nino is shaping up as one of the strongest on record, possibly a "super El Nino," with subsurface Pacific warm-water anomalies around 7°C above normal versus a typical 2.5-3°C. He walks through the commodity and macro spillovers, explicitly flagging currency stress as a key channel to watch — relevant for an EM trader given Brazil and India are the two most exposed origins.

**Key points**
- Nino 3.4 subsurface anomalies are far above typical El Nino thresholds; peak expected Oct-Dec 2026 with effects lingering through 2027 and into early 2028.
- Drier Southeast Asia/India (monsoon risk), wetter but heat-stressed Brazil; sugar, corn, ethanol and soybean markets most exposed; Australia wheat also dry.
- Panama Canal, Rhine, Danube, Bab-el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz all face simultaneous disruption risk — a scenario not seen historically, threatening global trade/logistics flow.
- Higher energy demand (AC load) in Asia and hotter/drier conditions raise natural gas and oil demand sensitivity; hydro power favorable in Brazil/N. America but at risk in Southeast Asia and Southern Africa.
- Historical analogs: 1877 (super El Nino, global famine), 1997-98, 2015-16; current event compared unfavorably against all three.

**FX / rates implications**
- Guest explicitly names USD/BRL, USD/INR and USD/JPY as currency pairs likely to see amplified, commodity-driven stress/volatility as El Nino intensifies — worth monitoring for EM Asia and LATAM books.
- Agricultural supply shocks (India sugar/monsoon risk, Brazil cane belt) could pressure food inflation and terms-of-trade for INR and BRL; a genuine super El Nino risks tail moves akin to historical famine-linked events.
- Broader risk-sentiment channel: simultaneous canal/strait disruptions (Panama, Suez-adjacent Hormuz/Bab-el-Mandeb, Rhine, Danube) would tighten global trade and could spike oil/gas and freight costs, an indirect USD/risk-off driver relevant to EM carry trades.

**Watch list**
- NOAA/Climate Prediction Center and Japan Meteorological Agency El Nino ensemble updates for peak timing (currently forecast Oct-Dec 2026).
- India monsoon progression into the sugar-cane belt; Brazil second-crop (safrinha) planting conditions moving into 2027.
- Panama Canal reservoir/transit capacity and Strait of Hormuz status as compounding logistics risk into 2027.

episodes.title: Cut to the Chase! What’s next for equities in August?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A Standard Chartered market update on US equities hitting a new all-time high after a rare negative July, driven by de-escalation hopes in the Middle East and strong Q2 earnings. While the direct focus is DM equities, the drivers (long-term US rates, Middle East risk, and US election-cycle volatility) are core global risk-sentiment channels relevant to any macro trader.

**Key points**
- S&P 500 made a new all-time high, surpassing its early-June record; July 2025 saw a rare slight decline, the first negative July in a decade.
- Middle East tensions pushed US 10-year yields above 4.7% in July on inflation fears; a reported imminent US-Iran deal and de-escalation headlines have since pulled yields lower, supporting equities.
- StanChart's back-testing shows every 25bp rise in cost of capital creates a 3-4% potential equity valuation impact.
- Over 60% of S&P 500 companies have reported Q2 earnings, with 85% beating estimates versus a historical average of about two-thirds; full-year 2025 earnings growth is tracking above 30%, with ~15% growth expected in 2026.
- Midterm election years historically bring above-average equity volatility in August-October.
- StanChart remains overweight US equities, favoring the Nasdaq (~10% further upside) on AI-driven tech earnings, and would buy weakness.

**FX / rates implications**
- US 10-year yield direction (above/below 4.7%) tied to Middle East de-escalation is a key input for USD/DXY and broad EM carry conditions; lower UST yields on de-escalation would ease pressure on EM Asia and LATAM rates and support carry trades.
- Continued global risk-on tone (record S&P highs, earnings beats) is broadly supportive of EM FX and risk assets via the standard risk-sentiment channel.

**Watch list**
- Progress on any US-Iran deal and Middle East de-escalation headlines.
- US 10-year Treasury yield trajectory relative to the 4.7% July peak.
- Ongoing Q2 earnings season beat rates.
- Volatility building into the US midterm elections in November, particularly August-October.

episodes.title: Ep90 Renewable Energy Works, So Why Isn't Asia Doing It? with Chan Yau Chong, Climate Finance Asia
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Chan Yau Chong of Climate Finance Asia discusses Hong Kong's slow renewables rollout and the broader Asian coal-fired power phase-out, arguing that mainstream financial institutions are hiding behind a narrow reading of "fiduciary duty" to avoid redirecting capital toward renewable energy. The conversation is a climate-policy and philanthropic-finance discussion rather than a markets one, but touches on capital allocation and energy-security themes relevant to Asian economies.

**Key points**
- Asia hosts roughly 40% of the world's coal-fired power plants, per Climate Finance Asia's research; the organization has published reports on coal transition drivers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Bangladesh and Pakistan, finding policy — not finance — is the main determinant of transition decisions in Indonesia.
- Hong Kong's grid remains dominated by fossil fuels despite a 2019 feed-in tariff scheme; officials aim to position the city as a green-finance hub, with a summit planned for September.
- Renewable energy costs are described as increasingly competitive with coal, and reliance on imported fossil fuels is framed as a geopolitical/energy-security risk.
- Guest expects material acceleration of Asian coal phase-out only over a 5-year (not 2-year) horizon.

**FX / rates implications**
No direct read-through to FX or rates markets; this is a climate-finance and ESG policy discussion, not a driver of currency or bond pricing. Any transmission is indirect and long-dated: faster coal phase-out and renewable buildout in Indonesia and Malaysia could eventually affect energy import bills and current-account dynamics relevant to IDR and MYR, but no near-term catalysts are identified.

**Watch list**
- Hong Kong green-finance summit in September.
- Further Climate Finance Asia reports on coal transition in Indonesia, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Pakistan.
- Pace of Hong Kong's 2030/2050 net-zero policy ambition, flagged as currently insufficient in the group's Paris-alignment tracking.

episodes.title: FX Moment: Dollar-Yen Bearish Push Needs US Data Validation Next
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
ING's Chris Turner and BI's Audrey Child-Freeman dissect the sharp Dollar-Yen reversal from 164 to below 155 over four sessions, driven by a softer post-FOMC dollar (July 29) and coordinated MoF/BOJ intervention. They frame near-term Dollar-Yen as a US-data story first, BOJ story second, then close with cross-EM/G10 conviction trades.

**Key points**
- Dollar-Yen fell from ~164 to ~155 intraday; market questioning durability of the move, intervention risk remains live.
- Fed September 16 meeting is pivotal: ~55-60% probability priced for a hike; ING house view is no hike if CPI prints soften toward 0.1% m/m, but resilient payrolls alone won't shift the call.
- Joint MoF/BOJ intervention was first since 1998 (Asian financial crisis); Turner says timing, not scale, made it effective — not a structural game-changer alone.
- IMF FX-regime rules cap intervention frequency (3 instances/6 months) before reclassification risk, potentially limiting a third intervention block until October.
- BOJ seen as behind the curve; step-up to tightening every 3 months (vs 6) is possible but fiscal dominance (loose fiscal, growth-first policy) caps Yen upside; ING targets USDJPY 158 (2026-end), 152 (2027-end).
- Cross-asset conviction: long NOK, AUD (targets AUD 0.73, EURNOK 10.80) on pro-risk, no-hike base case; USDCNH seen anchored near 6.70-7.00 low-vol range as PBoC manages surplus FX; constructive on EURHUF (350), Turkish lira carry, and Brazilian real (13% implied carry, election risk in October).

**FX / rates implications**
- USD path hinges on Fed September credibility risk — a hold amid resilient data could steepen long-end UST yields and turn bearish-dollar, a key channel into broad EM FX.
- PBoC's managed USDCNH stability functions as an anchor for regional EM Asia FX; Korean won volatility (dollar-won 1550→1430, 12% implied vol) still skewed toward dollar calls.
- LATAM carry (MXN, BRL) and EM carry (TRY, HUF) remain preferred yield plays if a stable-to-softer dollar persists.

**Watch list**
- September 16 FOMC and BOJ meeting; August/July US CPI prints before then; further intervention blocks against IMF's 3-instance rule; Brazil's October elections; Hungary's medium-term fiscal plan (~late October) tied to Euro-adoption path.

episodes.title: How ending TPS is squeezing workers, businesses and (soon) consumers
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
The Trump administration is winding down Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a humanitarian program shielding roughly a million foreign nationals from deportation; by year-end nearly all of the 17 originally covered countries could lose the designation. The episode traces the labor-market and consumer-price fallout through Florida's Haitian community, offering a US domestic labor-supply shock story rather than an EM FX/rates catalyst.

**Key points**
- TPS covered about 1.3 million people at the start of Trump's second term, with roughly 1 million working; 13 of 17 country designations have been terminated or targeted.
- Haiti's TPS termination affected over 300,000 people; Florida (Texas, New York, California, Georgia also large) hosts the biggest concentration of holders.
- TPS workers concentrated in construction, warehousing, healthcare, cleaning/maintenance — sectors with persistent US labor shortages at prevailing wages.
- Penn Wharton Budget Model analyst calls the scale of sudden work-authorization loss "unprecedented" for the US labor market.
- Home healthcare wages (currently $17-25/hr) are expected to rise as the eligible caregiver pool shrinks, with costs passed to consumers.
- Supreme Court ruled in June for the administration, rejecting claims that Haiti's TPS termination was racially motivated; administration cites national security/gang violence concerns.

**FX / rates implications**
- Minimal direct read-through for EM FX/rates; this is a US domestic labor-supply and services-inflation story (construction, healthcare, home-care costs), not a driver of USD, DXY, or EM currency flows.
- Marginal, indirect linkage: if mass TPS terminations contribute to sticky US services CPI, it could reinforce a modestly hawkish Fed reaction function, an angle worth noting only as tail context for USD/rates watchers.

**Watch list**
- Pace of remaining TPS terminations through year-end 2026 and any further Supreme Court or lower-court rulings.
- US CPI services/shelter and healthcare-cost components for early signs of wage pass-through from labor-supply tightening.
